title: Routing Information Protocol
summary: Describes the Routing Information Protocol, an existing way for gateways and hosts to exchange routing information, written as a basis for gateway software. It is a distance-vector protocol widely used in practice. It is historic, and later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723.

plainLanguage.summary: Neighbors tell each other how many steps it takes to reach various places, and everyone picks the shortest way. That is RIP, one of the earliest road-sharing systems for networks.

questions: how does the routing information protocol work
why is rip limited to 15 hops
subtitle: How early gateways swapped distance tables so every router could find the shortest path.

tldr.problem: Gateways and hosts on an IP network need to learn which neighbor to send each datagram to, and the widely used routing program routed had never been formally documented, so implementations disagreed in details.
tldr.mechanism: Each participant periodically tells its neighbors the distance (metric) to every destination it knows. Receivers add the cost of the network the update arrived on and keep the smallest total, with split horizon and triggered updates to limit routing loops.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is marked Historic and was later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723. It is limited to networks whose longest path is 15 hops, and it relies on counting to infinity to resolve some loops.

today: RFC 1058 is marked Historic and was later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723. It remains the original written description of RIP version 1.

sections.title: What RIP Is and What It Is Not
sections.content:
The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) documents an existing protocol for exchanging routing information among gateways and other hosts. It is based on the program routed from the 4.3 Berkeley Software Distribution, but several implementations disagreed in details, so the RFC combines features from various implementations. The author believes a program built from it will interoperate with routed and the other implementations he knows of.

RIP is meant as an interior gateway protocol (IGP) inside one autonomous system, for moderate-size networks using reasonably homogeneous technology. The RFC lists three limits: the longest path is 15 hops (assuming a cost of 1 per network), the protocol depends on counting to infinity to resolve certain unusual loops, and its fixed metrics are not suited to choosing routes by measured delay, reliability or load.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP is a way for the grown-up routers of one neighborhood to share road maps. It works for medium-sized neighborhoods but not for huge, complicated ones.

sections.title: Distance Vector Routing and Its Safeguards
sections.content:
In a distance vector algorithm every participant keeps a table with, for each destination, the next gateway and a metric. It sends neighbors its table. When an update arrives, the receiver adds the cost of the network it came over. It adopts the new route if the metric is smaller, or if the update comes from the gateway the current route already uses, even when the metric is larger.

Gateways that crash cannot announce it, so routes are timed out. RIP sends updates every 30 seconds and treats a route as dead after 180 seconds of silence. An unreachable destination is advertised with a metric of 16, which acts as infinity. The value is kept small on purpose: when a network vanishes, metrics can slowly climb in a loop called counting to infinity, and a small infinity ends that sooner.

Two defenses are specified. Split horizon stops a gateway from advertising a route back to the neighbor it learned it from, either by omitting it (simple split horizon) or by advertising it with metric 16 (poisoned reverse). Triggered updates make a gateway send changes almost immediately instead of waiting for the next regular update. Neither can fully prevent counting to infinity.

Poisoned reverse breaks two-gateway loops immediately but makes updates bigger. Implementors may choose simple split horizon or offer a configuration option.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone shouts how far away things are, and nobody trusts a road that a neighbor says goes back through yourself. If a road breaks, you say so right away instead of waiting for your turn to talk.

sections.title: RIP Messages
sections.content:
RIP runs over UDP. Each host's routing process sends and receives on UDP port 520. Unsolicited updates use port 520 as both source and destination, and replies go to the port the request came from. A silent process only listens, which suits hosts that are not gateways.

Every datagram has a command, a version (this document describes version 1) and a list of entries. Each entry carries an address family identifier (2 for IP), an IP address and a metric from 1 to 15, or 16 for unreachable. The entry part may appear up to 25 times in one datagram, and the maximum datagram size is 512 octets, not counting the IP and UDP headers. Large tables are simply split across several datagrams.

The commands are request (1) and response (2). Commands 3 and 4 (traceon, traceoff) are obsolete and are ignored, and 5 is reserved for Sun Microsystems. Version 0 datagrams are ignored; for version 1, any nonzero 'must be zero' field causes the whole message to be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A RIP message is a short form with a list of lines. Each line says 'this place is this many steps away'. The form is mailed to one special mailbox number, 520, on every router.

sections.title: Addresses, Subnets and Default Routes
sections.content:
RIP does not distinguish destination types. An address field can hold a host address, a subnet number, a network number, or 0.0.0.0 for a default route. When forwarding, a host uses the most specific match: host addresses first, then subnet or network, then the default.

Because subnet masks are normally known only for directly connected networks, border gateways must not send subnet routes outside the network they belong to. They send a single entry for the whole network instead, and hide host routes subsumed by a network route. A default route entry is strongly recommended but not required; implementations that do not support 0.0.0.0 must ignore such entries and must not pass them on.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can talk about a single house, a street, a whole town, or 'everywhere else'. They always use the most exact answer they have, and keep street details inside the town.

sections.title: Timers, Input and Output Processing
sections.content:
Every 30 seconds a complete response is generated for every neighboring gateway. To avoid all gateways synchronizing, implementations must either drive this timer from a clock unaffected by system load or add a small random offset each time it is set. Each route has a timeout of 180 seconds, reset whenever an update for it arrives. When it expires, or when the current gateway reports metric 16, the metric is set to 16, a 120-second garbage-collection timer starts, and a triggered response is signalled. The route is advertised as unreachable until that timer ends and the entry is deleted.

On input, a request for the whole table gets normal output processing, including split horizon. A request for specific destinations is answered with exact metrics and no filtering, since it is meant for diagnostics. A response must come from port 520 and from a neighbor on a directly connected network, and its own broadcasts must be ignored. For each entry, the new metric is MIN (metric + cost, 16). New routes with an infinite metric are not added.

Triggered updates are rate limited: after sending one, a timer is set for a random time between 1 and 5 seconds, and any further changes are combined into one update when it expires. A triggered update must include at least the routes whose change flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: Every half minute each router reads its list aloud to its neighbors. If a neighbor goes quiet for three minutes, the router decides the road is closed and tells everyone it is closed before forgetting it.

sections.title: Optional Control Functions
sections.content:
The last section describes administrative controls that are not part of the protocol itself, but which the RFC strongly recommends including. They exist because hosts are sometimes misconfigured and begin sending inappropriate information, and because sites may not want to advertise some networks to third parties.

Typical controls are a neighbor list, so a host accepts responses only from listed hosts, and lists of destinations to allow or disallow on a given interface in the incoming or outgoing direction. The RFC stresses that the protocol does not require these or any other controls.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can keep a list of neighbors it trusts and a list of places it is allowed to talk about, so one confused neighbor cannot mess up everyone's map.

items.label: request
items.desc: Asks the responder to send all or part of its routing table.

items.label: response
items.desc: Carries all or part of the sender's routing table.

items.label: reserved
items.desc: Used by Sun Microsystems; may be ignored.
